This study investigates the performance of two-layer neural networks using a specific activation function and uniform weight distribution in the input layer. It establishes a theoretical framework to understand how generalization errors affect a specific loss function as the dimensionality of the input space changes. Notably, this framework can be adapted for more complex scenarios, including those with restricted weight distributions. Furthermore, by applying this framework to a neural network with balanced binary classification and least-squares loss, we find that the optimal network capacity corresponds to the point of minimum validation loss and coincides with the crossover from underfitting to overfitting, even in high-dimensional settings within the hyperecube.

A significant dipole pattern in the direction of cosmic rays above 40 EeV has been discovered. To understand this phenomenon better, researchers analyzed dipolar patterns in the direction of cosmic rays between 4 and 62 EeV, accounting for variations in rates, arrival angles, and regional distributions. Employing a weighted approach, they found that the dipolar pattern increases with energy up to 8 EeV, then decreases beyond this point. This suggests a significant change in the properties of cosmic rays above this threshold, potentially indicating the influence of galactic magnetic fields or a shift in the origin of these cosmic rays, and highlighting the need for further investigation.

This passage outlines the foundation for results concerning the homogenization of thin films of minimal surfaces. The concept of geometric almost-periodicity, developed by Fugard and now applied to almost-minimal surfaces, is one key component. The author also introduces a novel form of uniform convergence that facilitates homogenization. These theoretical frameworks are complemented by another, more direct, approach to proving approximate periodicity, which offers an alternative to existing, more abstract methods.

This study investigates initial value problems associated with the charged Dirac field on FLRW spacetimes under 3-symmetric groups, extending prior work that examined charged Dirac fields on similar spacetimes without such symmetry. It demonstrates how a curved spacetime solution behaves as time progresses, specifically showing how it asymptotically approaches the solutions of the flat spacetime Dirac equation. Additionally, it derives precise time-dependent transformations of the causal kernels of the Dirac propagator as the spacetime transitions from matter- to radiation-dominated states.

We employ digital pathology to analyze whole tumor areas in H&E-stained tissue sections. Our method identifies and quantifies various cell types, including tumor infiltrating lymphocytes, within these sections. Our research involves closely examining multiple regions from 18 breast cancer and 18 colorectal cancer patient specimens, effectively tracking spatial patterns and immune cell interactions within the tumor microenvironment. Our work seamlessly combines computer vision and computational geometry techniques for this purpose, and we provide detailed mathematical descriptions of our algorithms, along with open-source software for replicability. Our software is publicly available at https://lymphnode.mit.edu/.

Cavity magnomechanics is a cutting-edge interdisciplinary field that combines magnon-polaron approach and quantum-optomechanics within magnon-sponon coupling. Its innovative system design enables a wide range of quantum-state engineering applications, including entanglement generation, coherent state preparation, andaman interaction. With the emergence of 2D magnetic materials, researchers can now build a type of microresonator called magnetic microcavities, which offers a versatile platform for various quantum technologies. In response to this development, we explore the possibility of applying the magnomechanical system to these microcavities, utilizing 2D magnetic materials as a quantum-optomechanical system that can be optically actuated and manipulated by a magnetic field. Our work demonstrates the generation of entangled states through the magnomechanical system in magnetic microcavities, which offers a wide range of potential applications in quantum technology due to the favorable properties of 2D magnetic materials, characterized by large magnomechanical coupling, optical nonlinearity, and mechanical resonance frequencies in the gigahertz range.

This research introduces a novel, fully automatic quadrupedal robot gait adaptation technique. The method is based on reinforcement learning, where the controller learns diverse gaits that can be adapted in real-time to various challenging tasks, such as navigating through obstacles and maintaining stability. The framework's core innovation lies in its ability to quickly adjust the learned policies through efficient gradient propagation. The framework comprises two main components: the first generates and fine-tails quadruped gaits to meet specific requirements, and the second enables real-time policy adaptation for quick and effective locomotion. The framework's additional features include a complex body-collision model and a contact-driven contact force estimator to improve the realism and adaptability of the quadruped's movements. The framework's outcomes highlight its ability to facilitate policy reuses and enable fast adaptation across a range of quadrupedal robots. The technique's effectiveness is demonstrated through successful robot walking in smooth and customized gaits, adjusted on-the-fly to different foot placements, and producing accurate body collisions and estimated contact forces, even with varying ground conditions. The technique also exhibits high generalizability and fast simulation times, allowing for rapid training and deployment of the policy on various robots.

Recent discoveries of low-luminosity active galactic nuclei (LLAGNs) in the hearts of early-type galaxies have brought these entities back into focus as key drivers of galaxy evolution through feedback processes. Due to the weak luminosity and close proximity of the LLAGN emission source, traditional observations using traditional instruments are insufficient for accurately determining key hydrodynamic parameters in the surrounding interstellar medium.  In order to overcome these challenges, an experiment utilizing unique observations of low-luminosity supermassive black hole activity in the heart of IC 3101, an early-type galaxy located within the Virgo cluster at a distance of 60 Mpc, has successfully mapped out the surrounding interstellar medium in greater detail.  Through the use of the Next Generation VLBI Explorer's (NEVER's) millimeter-wavelength polarimetric VLBI observations, researchers have successfully penetrated the inner 0.1 parsecs of the galaxy's center in a much more precise way than ever before observed with traditional instruments.  In order to gain insight into the physical processes occurring at the heart of the LLAGN system in the galaxy IC 3101, researchers have applied jet models to observational data and compared them to viscous, ballistic wind and Poynting-flux dominated wind models for the purpose of gaining insight into the life cycle of low-luminosity active galactic nuclei systems. This paper investigates the transient capabilities of reinforcement learning (RL) in optimizing linear quadratic regulators (LQRs), emphasizing the need for high model-free designs to adapt to changing systems in the RL context. A reduced-order virtual actuator addresses complex systems by replacing their original high-dimensional states with simpler representations, improving flexibility for RL model-learning without requiring complete system disclosure. A full-state feedback regulator, utilizing original state information, regulates the reduced-order system and is optimized for specific performance and robustness criteria. A data-driven reduced-order virtual actuator, learned through neural networks from initial responses and dynamical data, is then incorporated to regulate the original high-dimensional system, with optimization of the reduced-order performance regulator enabled by spectral analysis. Simulation results validate our suggestions, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach.

The SiD Detector calculated with the DD4HEP toolkit demonstrates enhanced calorimeter performance, with excellent jet energy resolution for jets spanning 0.1 to 1 TeV. The design incorporates fine-grained sampling, enabling precise energy deposition measurement in small cells. By employing a linear combination of strips and pads in the hadronic calorimeter, this fine granularity is achieved. The role of the ECAL and HCAL in jet energy reconstruction is examined through simulations of various jet composition types.

We conducted a comprehensive study of the Tononzintla 2 globular cluster, focusing on its metallicity and chemical composition. Chemical patterns were analyzed for 36 member stars across a wide spectral range ($4000-9000$ \AA), yielding a sample size fourth largest behind three other GCs. Tononzintla 2 exhibits significantly broader metallicity and chemical abundance spreads than typical globular clusters of high metallicity, and exhibits a strong $\alpha$-deficiency pattern, mirroring that seen in the Milky Way's outer disk stars. These findings suggest a complex star formation history involving an initial burst and prolonged chemical enrichment, potentially stretching over $\sim 50$ Myr.

To advance remote sensing using deep learning, our 'EarthNets' proposal aims to unify and facilitate access to a diverse collection of datasets, tools, and algorithms across various domains such as geostatistics, astronomy, and ecology. By standardizing the format of these datasets, we enable the seamless application and comparison of neural networks trained on one dataset to another, thereby promoting the remote sensing discipline's growth and fostering inter-disciplinary collaboration. 'EarthNets' encompasses multiple components, including diverse datasets, a versatile workflow for remote sensing tasks, and a standardised evaluation framework, all accessible through the 'EarthNets' platform at https://earthnets.org/.

Active matter research has experienced significant growth in recent years, with a focus on studying robust self-organized patterns in biological systems. This comprehensive review delves into the theoretical foundations of two-dimensional active nematics, beginning with a detailed description of the primary type of collective motion. Additionally, various aspects of two-dimensional active nematics are explored, including the effects of thermal fluctuations, energy dissipation relations, and dynamic correlations, as well as the spontaneous generation of topological defects and their role in driving the system's evolution. Furthermore, this review also investigates the emergence of a moving frame of reference in active nematics and discusses the presence of spontaneous flow rotations. Moreover, this study also delves into the effects of external driving and quiescent fluid environments on two-dimensional active nematics. Lastly, this review also considers the dynamics of a 2D active nematic membrane and explores its driving by thermal fluctuations and active stresses, as well as by active forces, and also discusses the presence of persistent flows in quiescent fluids and dynamic correlations in active media, with dynamic correlations exhibiting non-reciprocity.

This work focuses on using Deep Learning to identify regions of interest in medical imaging, particularly when dealing with medical masks, by analyzing data from machine learning and deep learning perspectives. We introduce a novel dynamic region partition approach that adapts to the spatial characteristics of input images, in contrast to conventional grid-based methods. This approach leverages a Convolutional Neural Network to process a single image and produces a partition that is then used to evaluate and converge on a detection result. Experimental findings across three datasets reveal that our method achieves superior performance in both accuracy and efficiency.

A systematic approach has been developed and implemented to apply two-pion data within a dispersion framework for computing hadronic light-by-light contributions. This method uniquely integrates low-energy constraints from chiral perturbation theory, leveraging its model-based predictions verified in numerical tests, with high-energy contributions estimated through operator product expansion. The framework's hadronic light-by-light effect calculation yielded a negative contribution of $-7.8(2)\times 10^{-10}$ to the muon anomalous magnetic moment, in alignment with existing calculations and clearly reflecting the negative hadronic light-by-light contribution calculated through lattice QCD.

Recent years have witnessed a significant surge in the adoption of deep learning, 
driven largely by the success of pre-trained models, which require minimal resource
intensive re-training for a variety of applications. This pre-trained model trend has
also extended into the field of programming, where models are trained to comprehend
and generate code, then applied with little re-training for tasks like auto-completion
and program synthesis. This research delves into the effectiveness of existing tools, 
also known as large language models (LLMs), designed to understand, process, and produce 
code across various programming languages. We evaluated several leading language models, 
including GPT-3, CodeBERT, and Transformers, across multiple programming languages 
like Python, JavaScript, and Java. Through comprehensive testing, we assessed their 
performance on multiple tasks, including code classification, defect prediction, 
software clustering, code completion, and program synthesis. Our findings indicate 
that pre-trained models can indeed outperform traditional machine learning approaches, 
yet code-specific models consistently exhibit superior accuracy compared to general 
language models in code-related applications.

Recent theories on galactic formation suggest that varying disc/spheroid configurations arise from varying formation processes. To clarify the effect of variegated dissipation on formation differences, we conducted a series of high-resolution simulations of variegated disc collapse. We used this to train a neural network and developed a disc/spheroid classification algorithm. We found that the variegated disc component and total disc fraction can be accurately identified, but the variegated disc fraction is a primary factor in classification. Additionally, our results show that spheroid suppression occurs when the variegated disc component is present, and disc fractions can distinguish galactic components effectively. These findings align with previous research and suggest that a single, continuous formation process can explain the diversity of galactic discs and spheroids.

Calculating atmospheric aerosol optical depth is crucial for uncalibrated, large-scale photometry systems that are frequently used in astronomical observations. A novel, calibration-free algorithm has been developed for deriving this crucial parameter using wide-field photometry data. By leveraging the relative flux variation of bright stars across multiple bands, this approach isolates atmospheric attenuation and assumes that over an expansive field of view, atmospheric effects are uniform. Applying this algorithm to the PanSTARRS dataset reveals a distinct pattern of declining aerosol optical depth with increasing elevation, consistent with theoretical predictions. Additionally, when paired with atmospheric modeling, it enables accurate deduction of sea-level aerosol optical depth. A comparative analysis with authoritative aerosol optical depth datasets validates the reliability of this method. Its straightforward implementation and rapid execution make it well-suited for extensive photometric datasets, atmospheric scale studies, and real-time atmospheric monitoring.

This research enhances the Graphical Lasso framework by integrating latent variables to improve model expressiveness and flexibility in complex problem settings. By introducing a novel extension that captures hidden patterns, the modified model enables precise prediction and accurate graph estimation even when crucial variables are not directly observable. Performance on both synthetic and real-world data outperforms the standard Graphical Lasso method and other existing latent variable models in both density prediction and precision matrix estimation.

We conducted a comprehensive analysis of the XMM-Newton X-ray observations of Cyg9-53A, a pre-main-sequence star in the Massive Young Star Cluster 30D. Our data revealed varying levels of observed X-ray luminosity, ranging from approximately 10^31 to 10^33 erg s^-1 over a two-year period. To interpret these X-ray emissions, we developed two distinct models: one attributed to magnetic activity, and the other to accretion processes. Initially, we established a baseline model consisting of two components - one representing hot corona, and the other a disk with two free-electron temperatures, and found that it adequately fitted the X-ray spectra collected in 2012. However, when applying this baseline model to the 2011 and 2012 X-ray spectra, we observed the emergence of enhanced hot component luminosity coinciding with periods of elevated stellar X-ray output. Furthermore, an alternative model incorporating time-dependent variations in the disk's absolute size and brightness provided an even better fit to the disk component, yielding a maximum absolute disk size of around 2 R_* (where R_* represents the stellar radius) and a corresponding brightness temperature of approximately 2.6 x 10^17 cm^-2 at around 2 x 10^4 K.

In music production, audio software enables engineers to adjust individual audio components of a track by automatically detecting and extracting vocal components, a process known as voice separation. However, this extraction can be hindered by background noise, resulting in inaccurate pitch assessment. To address this issue, a two-step approach is presented in this paper that estimates and removes background noise before determining the speech fundamental frequency. A cycle-cut method is used to model the noise and background speech as an image, and a minimum-cut algorithm is applied to separate the speech and noise components. This is followed by a pitch detection algorithm that utilizes a bank resonance strip to accurately determine the speech fundamental frequency. The approach has been incorporated into a module that automatically separates voice components from a music track, and it has been shown to enhance pitch accuracy in the presence of background noise.

The regularized Anderson acceleration method has proven effective in addressing non-smooth, non-monotone fixed-point problems due to its stability. In a recent study, the researcher investigated the robustness of the method by modeling its behavior using stochastic models and analyzing its randomization. However, a key concern emerged: the need to provide regularization for each iteration, which hinders efficient implementation as it involves costly nonlinear optimization. This led to a novel dynamic vector interpolation formula-based Anderson acceleration, dubbed DWIFOB, that directly addresses a fixed-point problem without requiring additional regularization. This approach has shown remarkable results, demonstrating superior performance and stability compared to its regularized Anderson acceleration counterpart. Moreover, the refinement step within DWIFOB can be omitted, making it more efficient and practical. Extensive numerical experiments confirmed the reliability and effectiveness of DWIFOB across various test problems.

Building upon a recent post-Higgs discovery comparison of predicted lightest Higgs boson masses in the Minimal Superstandard Model (MSM) and the Minimal Next-to-Minimal SUSY SM (NMSSM), this work introduces an additional neutrino sector to the NMSSM. It is observed that with free sequestered A terms, NMSSM predictions for the lightest Higgs boson mass are reduced, an effect amplified when neutrinos are included, resulting in even lower predicted masses.

Recent breakthroughs in Neural Architecture Search have accelerated the design of superior models, however most previous studies have been done under controlled, static environments. This research aims to extend this work by releasing the first open-source release for continuous neural architecture search, allowing search processes to run for extended periods without interfering with their own outcomes. A specific multi-objective approach is proposed, based on the use of a continuous representation of architectures as inductive bias functions, which are optimized using a variant of the Bayesian optimization framework adapted for continuous domains. A corresponding algorithm is formulated, enabling efficient training and search processes that balance performance and complexity. A corresponding toolkit is designed to support these procedures, allowing for quick and reliable model design. A series of experiments demonstrate the proposed algorithm's reliability and produce some of the best known architectures on established benchmarks, outperforming previous methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency, while also setting a new standard for simultaneous multi-objective optimization in neural architecture search.

The millimeter-wave (mmWave) frequency band offers vast bandwidth for diverse applications. Research indicates that multi-user communication via beamforming achieves considerable gains in systems with multiple antennas at the transmitter. This research examines practical multichannel mmWave beamforming systems and assesses the impact of various factors on performance and complexity. By simplifying the radio model, we develop an efficient beamformer design. Our results reveal the importance of high-quality channel estimation and accurate signal representation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a single high-gain antenna at the receiver yields similar performance to multiple low-gain antennas, and that a simple single-bit feedback mechanism can enable effective beamforming.

This investigation arises from the observation that Federated Distillation (FD) is a common FD setting due to FD Averaging (FDA)'s shortcomings in generating diverse gradients. FD enables a local model to be distilled by the server using clean data, but at the expense of substantial communication costs, particularly when model sizes continue to grow. Furthermore, communication efficiency can be compromised when the server employs a powerful teacher model with a large number of parameters. To address these challenges, Compressed Federated Distillation is proposed, a method that efficiently communicates by compressing both the teacher model and client gradients. Specifically, the teacher model is compressed via pruning and quantization, while client gradients are compressed via the Personalized Stochastic Karcher Mean (PSKM) scheme. Notably, PSKM minimizes distance between compressed gradients while adapting to each client's preferences. Theoretical analysis proves that Compressed Federated Distinction converges to the optimal solution at a rate of O(1/sqrt(N)), where the theoretical error depends on pruning and quantization errors. Experimental results on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 demonstrate that with less than 5% model retention rate, Compressed Federated Distinction reduces FD's communication requirements and achieves comparable or superior accuracy, requiring 5x fewer communications. Similarly, PSKM achieves at least 95% of global models' performance on the CIFAR-100 dataset with just 5% of communications.

In wireless body-area networks, the interaction of various wearable sensors is facilitated by a communication area where contextual information is shared. To increase the efficiency of this communication, a contextual data transmission approach, such as the contextual service discovery assisted dynamic orchestration (SDADO), has been introduced. This approach is context-driven and utilizes wearable services to optimize performance. Studies utilizing the SDADO-based model have shown substantial improvements in overall system performance, specifically ending-to-end latency and data transmission capacity. This paper outlines two operational protocols for the SDADO-based service model, examines the effectiveness of context-based data transmission, and compares the effectiveness of different context types for improving end-user delivery performance.

This research examines the exponential stability of a damped wave equation set on a specific type of directed graph with multiple branches. All branches meet at a central point and have no reflective boundaries. We prove that the system's stability is determined by the minimum of two factors: the difference between the highest and lowest frequency-critical damping values on the graph, and the difference between the highest and lowest reflection coefficients along the graph's perimeter.

A new type of symmetry breaking, not previously observed, occurs within a specific interaction known as the longitudinal channel, resulting from the effect of an external magnetic field on a charged particle's movement, characterized by its cyclotron frequency, denoted by the symbol omega-c, which is greater than zero, within a charged relativ field theory that involves a zero mass particle interacting with both a vector particle and a scalar particle.

Recent discoveries have shown that midinfrared dynamical hyperbolic materials can exhibit unusual properties and may be used in advanced technological applications, such as super-resolution imaging, negative refractive index phenomena, and hyperbolic photonic crystal laser technology. In this study, we find that MTl4Te3 is a midinfrared dynamical hyperbolic material and simulate the hyperbolic photonic crystal laser based on this material for the first time. Our results show that by adjusting MTl4Te3's thickness and gold mirror spacing, we can control the lasing threshold threshold and laser emission spectrum, and that this control is directly related to the photonic band structure. Moreover, MTl4Te3's midinfrared lasing emission has significant potential for spin torque equipment and spin devices, thanks to its unique properties such as high nonlinearity, simple composition, and negligible absorption loss.

To achieve long-term goals in complex optimization tasks, advanced systems need a comprehensive understanding of the individual components and their significance.
Usually, this understanding is developed by considering how components are ranked against each other.
However, utilizing only ranking data can lead to incomplete understanding and a poorly characterized solution space.
This study proposes an alternative approach by learning a utility function using expert knowledge, which is distinct from pairwise result preferences.
Specifically, experts define the relative importance of different system aspects using a structured framework, and we present a formal model for this process.
We apply the model to optimize Markov decision processes, and show that it enables solving more difficult and large-scale problems that were previously challenging, while also improving the quality of solutions in standard problems.

As trained reinforcement learning agents grow more complex, accurately predicting their behavior becomes essential but also challenging. Traditional methods, based on modeling reward and dynamics p(rewards, transitions), are often ineffective due to their reliance on precise specifications and the tendency of rewards to be influenced by minor changes in policy. A more promising approach, described in this study, involves using sequence-to-sequence models to implicitly capture the underlying dynamics of an agent's actions. An efficient implementation is achieved through the Sequence to Sequence Model for Action Prediction (S2S MAP) architecture, which enables accurate prediction of future states and can generalize to new situations. Comparative results, including those from major reinforcement learning benchmarks, highlight the advantages of this approach over rival methods.

This research investigates how to adjust the characteristics of a herringbone lattice by incorporating different perturbations into the Hamiltonian, focusing on modifying both bandgap and bandwidth properties. By analytically deriving expressions for band edges, our findings show that by applying varying perturbations, both bandgap and bandwidth can be simultaneously manipulated, unlike the typical scenario where a specific type of perturbation only affects the bandgap or bandwidth. These results reveal a means to tailor the electronic structure of herringbone materials, such as TMD monolayers and carbon nanotubes, for exploration and validation of both analytical and numerical methods.

A key challenge in reinforcement learning (RL) is efficiently navigating changing environments while adhering to specified risk constraints. To address this, we develop restart-based algorithms for both policy search and dynamic programming, enabling the efficient learning of risk-sensitive policies in fast-changing environments. These algorithms incorporate the entropy of outcomes from individual trajectories to account for risk, and through the application of the entropy bonus, we ensure exponential concentration of results, thereby achieving risk-sensitive results. The resulting risk-sensitive policies can be computed online in nearly the same time frame as their risk-neutral equivalents, making them suitable for real-time decision-making in changing environments. The theoretical analysis, supported by numerical experiments, illustrates the versatility and effectiveness of our restart-based algorithms for a broad range of risk-sensitive policy design and evaluation tasks.

In January 2021, we introduced the first comprehensive dataset of publicly accessible Jira projects, comprising four years of issue tracking data. Each project includes metadata, issues, comments, and users. This work presents the results of further analysis of the introduction period of these projects and presents a case study involving Netflix. The introduced data will enable researchers to perform a range of additional studies, such as cross-domain analysis, various analytical investigations, and extensions of existing research. The dataset is available for download on GitHub under a CC-BY-4.0 license, with project access credentials provided in the supplementary materials of this paper.

This paper investigates Aggregation Functions in distributed machine learning, with a concentration on weighted power-p mean (WPM), a non-linear aggregation method that encompasses other related functions like arithmetic and geometric means. Unlike standard linear aggregation, WPM enables more versatile learning, yet it poses greater challenges due to its non-linear nature, particularly in terms of noise tolerance. Our research centers around developing a novel non-linear aggregation approach that is both robust and efficient for weighted arithmetic geometric means, and we demonstrate its application in a variety of distributed learning settings, achieving optimal convergence rates in scenarios involving heterogeneous data and models. Our theoretical analysis is supported by numerical experiments that validate the efficiency and resilience of our aggregation approach, and we make the code available online to facilitate replication and further investigation.

A pivotal aspect of developing advanced technology across multiple disciplines is the ability to manipulate and control individual atoms with precision, specifically through the manipulation of their internal states and external positions. The potential for this capability is vast, from quantum computing to atomic precision measurements. The proposed invention consists of a system that uses a single atom trapped within an optical dipole trap created by a pair of optical counter-propagating beams, coupled with a micro-prism that features a narrow slit. By adjusting the position of the atom within this setup, the experiment can demonstrate a significant alteration in the atom's emitted fluorescence due to the interference of evanescent waves, thereby proving that the device can serve as a gate that controls an atom's emitted light.

In valuated oriented graphs arranged in a grid format, specific paths known as 'zigzags' possess distinct highest and lowest points marked by peaks and valleys. The term 'closed upper set of a word' refers to a collection of points in such a graph, encompassing and exceeding a specified word. This study examines the local and global characteristics of closed upper sets of words within "nice" valuated oriented graphs, characterized by a specific labeling system. By analyzing these characteristics, it's possible to determine whether an edge within the grid meets this distinction, thereby allowing computation of distances between words within these 'nice' graphs, thereby extending a significant concept originating from "tropical geometry".

We've developed a novel, theory-free approach to analyzing polymers in their various states. 
Using a powerful representation, the polymer is mapped to a sequence of basic building blocks, called monomers, which capture its essential characteristics. 
This approach considers all possible arrangements of the monomers and their interactions, even when the polymer is split apart. 
By focusing on the shared patterns among different molecules, we can represent a wide range of monomers effectively, regardless of their size or complexity. 
As a result, this method enables us to identify and categorize the fundamental building blocks behind every polymer molecule, ultimately leading to a more accurate and compact representation. 
Using our own set of rules for comparing molecules, we can verify that our method is consistent and efficient, allowing us to represent even the most complex polymers using a relatively small number of basic building blocks. 
Finally, we've demonstrated the effectiveness of our method in predicting various properties of small polymers, achieving a level of accuracy that is comparable to or exceeds that of top-performing supervised learning approaches, but with significantly less need for labeled data.

Multipe patient ventilation using one ventilator can be an effective strategy to alleviate ventilator shortages during a pandemic, such as COVID-19. A novel approach, dynamic sequential high-frequency oscillation, allows multiple patients to share a single ventilator while maintaining individualized tidal volumes. However, its impact on patient mechanics and gas exchange requires further study. A study was conducted to compare dynamic sequential high-frequency oscillation with conventional bi-level positive airway pressure/continuous positive airway pressure ventilation in healthy subjects. A total of 12 volunteers participated in a single-blind trial, where they were randomly assigned to receive either dynamic sequential high-frequency oscillation or conventional bi-level positive airway pressure/continuous positive airway pressure ventilation for two hours. During this period, their respiratory mechanics and gas exchange were continuously evaluated, and no adverse events occurred. Our findings suggest that dynamic sequential high-frequency oscillation produces similar respiratory mechanics and gas exchange outcomes to conventional bi-level positive airway pressure/continuous positive airway pressure ventilation, indicating its potential for safe use in multipe patient ventilation scenarios, such as those seen in a pandemic like COVID-19, provided proper patient training and careful patient selection are in place.

Rational maps exhibiting two distinct fixed points with specific dynamics behaviors were analyzed, exhibiting symmetry around these fixed points. A generalization to maps with multiple symmetry groups was developed, with dynamics remaining similar outside periodic orbits under all symmetry transformations. It was found that within these symmetry transformations, periodic orbits follow straightforward patterns, with depths tied to group theory principles. It was also demonstrated that existing methods for mapping classes under conjugation remain valid, with some modifications, for this new class of rational maps.

In a general framework for high-dimensional Bayesian regression models with l prior on coefficients, we determine the posterior contraction rates for the model's parameters and dimension under both known and unknown error variance scenarios. These findings are applicable to a broad class of models, including Bayesian Gaussian Ridge, Lasso, and $\L_0$ posterial concentration, and show that considering unknown error variance impacts contraction rates but has variable effects on posterior dimension concentration.

This research examined how different machine tool factors influence surface roughness values in machining operations, and identified the most impactful variables through analysis of experimental data collected using a Taguchi L9 x3^5 design. The experiment varied the effects of different tools on surface roughness and analyzed the resulting data to create performance prediction models and assess the reliability of the findings. The analysis indicated that surface roughness values are most influenced by the type of tool used, followed by feed rate, tool approach speed, and depth of engagement. Predictive models were created for different machining operations, including milling with both end and face mill tools, and drilling, with the best model having an R-squared value of 0.9736, suggesting a high degree of accuracy in the L9 x3^5 design for identifying the variables with the greatest effect on surface roughness.

Let $X$ be a metric space with finite Ahlfors regular conformal dimension, where the given distance is of graph nature. We provide a counterexample illustrating that removing a sufficiently small proportion of edges from the underlying graph can result in a new distance that is quasi-isometrically conformally equivalent to the original distance.

Hadron nature mixing is investigated in the context of isoscalar mesons $h(980)$ and $h(1185)$. Hadronic production and decay processes are considered alongside the parameterized field Lagrangian that accounts for the mixing of $s$-$\eta'$ and $s$-$\eta$ interactions, as well as the intrinsic mixing of $h(980)$ and $h(1185)$. The analysis employs physical observables such as production cross sections and branching ratios in hadronic decays to derive the complex eigenvalues of the mass matrix that describes the mixing of these mesons. Various production processes, including $J/\psi \to \eta' rh(980)$, $J/\psi \to \eta' rh(1185)$, $J/\psi \to \eta h(980)$, $J/\psi \to \eta h(1185)$, $e^+e^- \to \eta' h(980)$, $e^+e^- \to \eta' h(1185)$, $e^+e^- \to \eta h(980)$, $e^+e^- \to \eta h(1185)$, $\rho \to \eta' h(980)$, $\rho \to \eta' h(118

Our new signature forgery detection system leverages 3D and reoriented template matching to assess distinctiveness, complexity, and repeatability of signature templates. These factors inform the system's capacity to identify forged signatures and improve its accuracy. A built-in optimizer adjusts the parameters of the system to maximize its performance.

The low-energy effective couplings of the K3 heterotic string are constrained by supersymmetry, enabling an in-depth analysis of the string theory's effective coupling landscape. Utilizing supersymmetry constraints and recent findings on moduli stabilization, we investigate effective couplings under supersymmetry breaking conditions, including gauge mediation. Notably, we find that supersymmetry constraints limit the magnitude of loop-level couplings, even when the vacuum state involves supersymmetry breaking. This reveals a stronger set of effective coupling bounds compared to non-supplementary scenarios.

We introduce a new analytical method to compute quantum correlation functions in large, active many-body systems by incorporating the effects of quantum and thermal fluctuations. Our approach reformulates correlation functions as path integrals in imaginary time. A key breakthrough is expressing active terms as derivatives with respect to path variables. Employing a saddle-point approximation yields correlation functions that can be analytically computed. Our method is versatile and can be applied to systems characterized by both continuous and discrete paths. By doing so, we bypass the limitations of traditional stochastic methods that struggle to derive accurate correlation functions. Our approach also facilitates an efficient computation of active correlation functions through path-schematized Feynman diagrams. We further develop a perturbative framework to account for thermal and quantum fluctuations beyond the dominant active terms. To illustrate our method, we apply it to active Bohm-Pauli and Pauli blocking Feynman diagrams.

A comprehensive computer simulation of a galaxy's chemical and structural development, incorporating turbulent motion, reveals that the rate at which nitrogen forms is not constant but varies with the amount of oxygen produced. This contradicts previous models where nitrogen formation was unchanging, regardless of other elements formed. The simulated galaxy exhibits an increasing nitrogen-to-oxygen ratio as the galaxy evolves, with the primary cause being galaxy turbulence accelerating nitrogen's formation. Computer simulations show that turbulence increases nitrogen's self-interaction forces, but has no such impact on oxygen, leading to O and N atoms accumulating differently in the simulated galaxy. The same effect is observed in galaxies in our observable universe. The galactic model accurately replicates the nitrogen-to-oxygen trends found in stellar populations and galaxies, notably explaining a observed decrease in this ratio at very low oxygen abundances.

Recent breakthroughs in natural language processing (NLP) research have been greatly influenced by the extensive multilingual context in which it is being conducted. Although the current landscape of multilingual NLP is characterized by an abundance of data and models, there are areas that require additional consideration, particularly in data representation, multilingual text alignment, low-resource scenarios, and NLP applications for under-resourced languages. These areas are crucial in addressing real-world challenges faced by diverse linguistic environments and multilingual societies. We identify the need for continued NLP research to address the complexities of multilingual data representation, data alignment, data collection, and application development for languages that are often overlooked. Our goal is to highlight existing opportunities in NLP research that are essential for effectively supporting multilingual society and underserved languages, while also recognizing the data-driven NLP landscape.

The analysis of networked data is highly effective in identifying complex biological signals embedded within noise and bias. Specifically, biological data is often represented in the form of graphs where nodes and edges encapsulate both quantitative and qualitative information. Numerous graph-based metrics are employed in biological research to extract meaningful patterns and relationships. This review focuses on the diverse application of such metrics in the analysis of biological signals, beginning with an examination of fundamental graph metrics and their significance in biological contexts. It subsequently explores the practical uses of these metrics across various biological domains, including cellular and molecular biology, developmental biology, neurobiology, and evolutionary biology.

Researchers have developed a set of constraints on the Left-Right Symmetric Model, specifically within its self-conjugate bi-doublet sector, via analysis of various phenomena including particle collisions, neutrino oscillations, and the behavior of stars in various phases of development. While previous studies focused on collision data, this investigation centers on the impact of stellar observations, particularly the dynamics of massive stars in various phases, to limit the model's parameter space. The analysis reveals that the lack of detected axions, resulting from the cooling patterns of X-ray stars, significantly restricts the model's parameter space, outputting a minimum mass threshold of 0.89 GeV, alongside other limits set by neutron stars and star in the CE phase, result in a minimum mass of 1.3 GeV, whereas massive stars in the CE phase impose an upper limit of 1.15 GeV,

This paper introduces the Graph Privacy Advisor, an innovative graph privacy classifier tailored for pre-processing images to assess their privacy-related attributes. Unlike conventional graph models that rely on basic operations like node aggregation and neighbor counting, our approach leverages a graph neural network to effectively consider more complex relationships between nodes and their neighbors. By utilizing SIFT key-points as nodes and defining edge weights based on spatial distances and intensity differences, we've developed the Graph Privacy Advisor, which was tested on a substantial dataset consisting of 1,500 manual labels across various concepts like privacy and privacy violations. The method's performance significantly outperforms other baseline models, with notable improvements in accuracy, especially in classifying images with privacy-related attributes, and also demonstrates better generalization and concept transferability compared to existing approaches.

In recent research, it was proposed that quantum fluctuations can cause a flow of entropy within the radiation field, contradicting traditional thermodynamic principles. This model, however, relied on an inaccurate application of quantum statistical entanglement, leading to spurious results. We present two new theories, one for a pair of cavities and another for a cavity containing two-level atoms, that accurately capture the entropy flow arising from quantum statistical entanglement among radiation modes. Our analysis reveals that for the two-level atoms, entanglement-induced entropy flows outwards from the atomic system, whereas in the cavity model, the entanglement can actually facilitate a decrease in entropy within the cavity. This latter effect has significant implications for information processing and error correction processes.

Measurements involving photon-tagged jets and inclusive jets in Pb+Pb collisions are reported, where a photon with a specific energy range and rapidity was paired with a jet of various categories. A significant observation was the differential modification of photon-tagged jets and inclusive jets based on their transverse momentum, with no evident influence of final-state interactions on the pairs with higher transverse momentum. Moreover, the angular distribution and energy loss patterns of these pairs exhibited consistency. Furthermore, the presence of a significant increase in isolated photons surrounding inclusive jets with lower transverse momentum, with respect to pp collisions, was uncovered. These findings are in accordance with two-parton model predictions. Two such models, one assuming independent energy loss for both partons and the other considering the joint energy loss of both partons, were found to provide consistent descriptions of these data. Ultimately, these reports represent the initial comprehensive assessment of isolated particles interacting with jets in high-energy collisions.

The advancement in deep learning on large datasets has led to a growing need for efficient computational methods that can take advantage of the capabilities of low-precision hardware architecture, such as Tensor Cores in modern GPUs, with the current focus being on designing neural network architectures that can operate at lower precision levels, but a less explored area is the potential of novel computational methods to enhance performance and precision efficiency, we investigate the effectiveness of matrix multiplication shortcuts on precision efficiency and performance, we develop an version of Wilson Fermions in TWISTED MASS formulation suitable for low-precision hardware, we evaluate the precision efficiency of our fermions through comparison with other low-precision approaches and demonstrate the feasibility of Wilson fermions in TWISTED MASS formulation on NVIDIA Tensor Cores, we achieve a 4x1 precision to computational cost ratio, with x4 accuracy at 2 BF16 costs, with 63% of the costs and 87% of the accuracy compared to full precision, we also explore and demonstrate a new approach to solving linear systems of equations using the Generalized Singular Value Decomposition, with results and costs analyzed, with implications for near-future computing on Tensor Cores.

Detecting hard X-rays emitted by the quiet Sun is a challenging task, mainly
due to a high level of background noise, a constraint that can be overcome with
the use of the (F)ocusable X-ray SpectroImager FOXSI, a specialized instrument
capable of quiet Sun observations. A pilot study has provided the first
successful detection of a quiet Sun in a specific 1 nm energy band, a feat
enabled by a combination of a specialized telescope and advanced data analysis
techniques. Under calm conditions, clear FOXSI images allow for a straightforward
realization of this detection. A more intricate case study involves a detected
quiet Sun observed under dynamic conditions, requiring a detailed data analysis
to confirm the finding. A novel image subtraction method, employing a
correlation approach, has been utilized to effectively remove background noise
and isolate weak quiet Sun signals, yielding an improved sensitivity in quiet
Sun observations.

Graph neural networks have become increasingly popular for analyzing social networks. However, their performance can be sensitive to fluctuations in graph composition, posing challenges for both training and testing purposes. To overcome these challenges, researchers proposed train- and test-time augmentation techniques for graph neural networks. Although augmentation has been utilized in other machine learning contexts, its application to social networks remains limited. Our work explores the effectiveness of augmentation in predicting user influence within social networks. We develop a novel augmentation strategy for social networks, incorporating a graph-based approach that balances performance and complexity. We compare our method with traditional train- and test-time augmentation techniques and demonstrate that augmentation is particularly effective for larger graphs, while being less beneficial for graphs with well-established connections. Our code is publicly available on GitHub.

We examine small deformations of solutions to the Euler-Arnold equations for Ising spins, which represent vacuum configurations in Euler-Heisenberg quantum electrodynamics. These variations correspond to solving a boundary value problem derived from maximizing an action functional, effectively reducing it to an elliptic system. We demonstrate that nontrivial solutions to this system do not exist within a certain range for the Euler-Heisenberg theory. Furthermore, we generalize the approach to scalar and sine-Sylvester models, also showing the absence of nonlinear elliptic systems' solutions. However, we find a nonlinear elliptic system with nontrivial solutions for the generalized generalized Euler-Heisenberg model.

A common issue in sensor-based pose estimation is the underestimation of errors due to limited noise correlations, which causes an overestimation of pose accuracy. In this research, we develop a novel approach for posenestry which considers broader correlations among errors, which results in improved noise estimates and, consequently, more accurate sensor readings. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our sensor-based pose calibration method on both laser scanner and IMU datasets using diverse environments, which shows that our approach yields better initial pose estimates and superior performance in subsequent tasks like SLAM and localization. Additionally, our technique is straightforward to implement and can be integrated into various other sensor fusion or estimation systems with minimal modifications.

This work envisions a multi-temperature universe with various energy scales, providing a framework to analyze the cross-sections of dark matter across different size ranges. By applying this concept, a connection is established between the non-resonant cross-section of dark matter and the non-resonant scattering processes of neutrinos and charged particles, which can be verified experimentally. Furthermore, the dark matter cross-section at larger scales is related to the interaction between neutrinos and charged particles, the minimum mass of dark matter particles is analogous to the minimum mass of neutrinos, and the density profile of dark matter mirrors the large-scale structure of the universe. Utilizing established bounds on neutrino interactions, the proposed framework rules out large-scale dark matter interactions greater than current constraints on bulk dark matter scattering of approximately $10^{-36}$ cm$^2$. Additionally, if the minimum mass of neutrinos exceeds 10-20 MeV, a significant portion of dark matter particles have a mass less than a keV, which is analogous to a warm dark matter scenario.

An investigation into the creation of two $W$ bosons with the same charge has been conducted utilizing proton-proton collision data at a 13 TeV energy level. This data was collected by the CMS experiment during 2016 and corresponds to an integrated luminosity of 36.1 fb$^{-1}$. Notably, the events in this study are distinguished by their high multiplicity of jet formation, a significant amount of transverse momentum carried by isolated charged particles, and a low level of missing transverse momentum in their momentum spectrum. An unusually high occurrence rate, specifically 3.3 standard deviations above what is predicted by standard models, was observed in the subset of data characterized by four isolated charged particles with substantial transverse momentum and substantial jet activity. Standard models are found to account for this occurrence rate, with supplementary analysis confirming that two other subsets of data are consistent with standard model predictions. Additionally, interpretations of this data within the framework of certain diquark-based new particle models are presented.

Generative adversarial networks (GANs) are used to develop a novel colorization method that better handles a broader range of colors compared to previous techniques. Unlike existing colorization GANs that focus on restoring colors and hues, our approach emphasizes hues as well as saturation, allowing for more accurate color reproduction. Moreover, our model is designed to be adaptable to various types of color data, including RGB, HSV, and LCMS, enabling its application in diverse color settings. A new colorization loss function is also introduced to enhance its performance. Experimental results demonstrate that our model outperforms previous colorization methods, particularly in accurately reproducing colors and hues.

We analyze the effectiveness of a previously proposed q-stepped quantum model for dark energy, called the $P(q)$ model, in addressing cosmological problems using only reasonable assumptions. Initially, it showed success in solving the cosmic coincidence problem, as it produced a declining equation of state of state, and could meet future predictions based on the accelerating expansion of the universe. However, when confronted with observational data from cosmic microlensing and non-flat models using $A_L=1$, it failed to constrain key parameters within observational limits. To address this limitation, we introduce an enhanced version of the $P(q)$ model, dividing each step into two levels to maintain decreasing equation of state. We analyze this improved model in detail, as it yields a least-fit value of approximately -1.02 for the current equation of state, consistent with data from cosmic microlensing. Furthermore, when confronting data from cosmic microlensing, it yields parameter constraints that are in line with previous data, while when analyzing non-flat models with $A_L=1$, it yields parameter constraints that are also consistent with data from cosmic microlensing.

One out of every 10 lines of existing software code remains actively maintained, a statistic that highlights the difficulty of sustaining shared files, especially in collaborative environments like software repositories, business processes, and publishing platforms, where maintenance often goes unmentioned. This study investigates how software repositories handle shared files, taking into account their individual contributions, collaborations, and maintenance efforts, and aims to boost collaboration by bringing transparent communication about individual and collective contributions, especially those related to maintenance, to the forefront. By manually examining the version histories of every shared file in the GitHub repository, we analyze individual and collective contributions, collaborations, and maintenance efforts, and the results show that: (RQ1) repo maintainers don't always notify others about removing their individual contributions, especially in cases where a file's name or content changes, or where a contributor removes their own code, and effective communication can be enhanced by introducing reminder functionality and allowing contributors to keep track of their own code, and (RQ2) there is no consistent approach to shared file maintenance across different repos, and a flexible versioning system could benefit from features like flexible retention policies, parallel maintenance, and content-based mergeable changes.

To resolve this uncertainty, this study applied two distinct kinematic techniques to identify potential extrinsic radial-velocity curves in its binary spectrum, specifically targeting the Ca I 6568 line and the Fe I feature at 6570.55 Å. Both techniques yield comparable results, indicating the existence of a third, non-gravitational binary element with a ratio of about 0.6 to 0.7 relative to the binary system itself, and moving at a 33 to 38 km per second velocity in relation to the binary's systemic velocity. This system consists of approximately 0.3 solar masses, moving in a 4 day orbit, likely in a nearly circular configuration. Spectral analysis of the binary reveals that the majority of its emission originates from the binary's disc, with an estimated temperature of 25000-30000 K. This study also explores whether a third element could be an active white dwarf using various arguments, and it's noted that a stellar companion is unlikely due to the high temperature of the system. This research shows that the Yamabe flow on compact manifolds may have local-in-time smooth solutions that do not maintain smoothness over time, even starting from smooth initial conditions. This finding validates the potential for the Yamabe flow to be sensitive to initial conditions, thereby supporting the possibility of chaotic behavior in certain manifolds under the Yamabe flow.

A prevalent approach in product recommendation involves learning a comprehensive aspect preference vector that captures product attributes, user history, and explicit ratings. However, due to the inherent aspect redundancy and user bias, this method can yield suboptimal recommendations. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel aspect preference enhancement (APE) module that user-centrically filters irrelevant aspect information and implicitly biases users. Furthermore, we present a gated aspect preference enhancement (GAPE) module that integrates multiple aspect representations and selects the most pertinent aspect to construct a robust aspect preference vector. Experimental results from two large-scale datasets demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, demonstrating significant improvements over existing baseline methods.

Application of formula (1.8) allows for efficient deduction of properties concerning partitions with specific constraints on their components, particularly their frequency occurrences. This approach is illustrated through several general formulas that bear resemblance to Andrews' part-by-part partitions concept. We utilize generating functions to rapidly obtain these general formulas, thereby allowing for the quick calculation of part-frequency restricted partition counts.

We investigate the optimal strategy for approximating functions under a given loss measure, considering both precise measurements and rough estimates of function values. To tackle this problem, we employ a probabilistic approach based on the assumption that the loss can be represented as a combination of weighted, independently distributed variables, corresponding to different basis functions. This leads to the conclusion that the weighted least squares method ensures stable and efficient approximations even when rough estimates are used, and moreover, it achieves optimal performance in the best possible r-dimensional subspace with an error bound proportional to the inherent error of that subspace, plus an additional error term resulting from differentiating between precise and rough estimates. Notably, we develop a stable algorithm for computing the weighted orthogonal projection, applicable in both finite and infinite-dimensional settings, which may be of broader interest due to its ability to handle ill-conditioned matrices and regularize them through special techniques.

The reaction rates and initial conditions are calculated for three distinct models of $X(3872)$ molecular, compact charmonium, and tetraquark forms, based on the relativistic hydrodynamic simulation outcomes. In analogy to their magnetic counterparts, we propose that disordered semiconductors like Si:P exhibit light-matter interactions that reflect their low-density electron structure, thereby exhibiting behavior akin to optical magnetism. By employing third-harmonic generation, we were able to uncover a type of interaction termed 'optoelectric birefrigeration' that arises from local magnetism. By measuring the intensity and phase of the light interaction, we were able to isolate and quantify this interaction, revealing its amplitude to be on the order of 10^-5, consistent with first-principles predictions.

Generalize standard OGS for the finite Coxeter groups of types $B_n$ and $D_n$ are represented as algebras with generators that satisfy specific exchange relations which are expressed in terms of the group's Coxeter length and descent set; this requires defining these parameters for elements within the group's half, based on its decomposition into two halves via its central element. The paper's main goal is to establish a recursive formula for these exchange relations for the group $B_n$ by utilizing a specific homomorphism that maps elements from the group's $D_n$ half to $B_{n-1}$'s Coxeter group, thereby enabling the derivation of our exchange relations' properties.

In scalar field theories with E symmetry, even when including quantum effects, the U(1) current retains its conservation status despite the presence of explicit symmetry breaking terms. This is because such terms can be in the form of a total time derivative. Using this U(1) current, we define a topological current, J, which in two-dimensional E_u(1)\E_0U(1) invariant theories, includes a Dirac string current resulting from a nontrivial phase of the order parameter. An additional current, \tilde{J}, emerges when including explicit symmetry breaking terms with an anisotropic U(1) group in two and four dimensions, leading to a link between this current and a topological term in the action, specifically a Wess-Zumin term. Furthermore, we investigate the consequences of including this effective Wess-Zumin term in the action of certain two-dimensional theories, such as the O(2) sigma model, a free SU(N) gauge theory, and an effective action describing a system of anyons.

This research introduces a novel task decomposition approach that integrates both task-irrelevant information and expert robot demonstrations to facilitate robust robot learning. By utilizing a hierarchical Bayesian model, individual data points are assigned relevant tasks to filter out various confounding elements, enabling the development of a more reliable policy. We present a novel assignment framework that efficiently distributes data points to their corresponding tasks, preventing overloading any single task. Through comprehensive simulation studies using a physical robot, we demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in handling unanticipated challenges and facilitating robot learning from example traces in complex real-world environments.

The whisker topology $\Xi$ on a space $X$ extended to $\tilde{X}_H$, the Hausdorfization of $X$ with respect to homotopy through paths, is studied in relation to the lasso topology. A proof that these two topologies coincide for tree-like spaces is presented, and it's shown that they don't coincide for certain biped spaces. Additionally, examples of path-connected spaces where the whisker and lasso topologies on $\tilde{X}_H$ are distinct are provided.

A novel, multi-stage framework for motion planning in complex, unknown environments has been developed. This research concentrates on two-stage motion planning that integrates deep reinforcement learning, specifically within the motion execution stage, a distinct process from conventional methods. The proposed framework leverages deep reinforcement learning to master motion execution, while a multi-objective evolutionary algorithm handles the motion planning stage, using a set of high-level goals to generate a plan. This plan is then executed by a deep reinforcement learning model trained through deep Q-network, with no adjustments made during execution. The framework's motion planning stage employs a multi-objective evolutionary algorithm to efficiently navigate through the search space, demonstrating its ability to uncover optimal solutions and adapt to unexpected events. Comprehensive experiments were conducted in simulated and real-world settings, and the results indicated that this two-stage framework matches the performance of state-of-the-art alternatives.

This process results in a central black hole mass at the end of typical star formation timescales that can be up to 100 times greater than what is predicted by BHFE models.
